articles.title: Arctic power play gives top US adversary new opening with Russia as US stakes grow
articles.summary: China launched seasonal container service to Europe via Russia's Arctic Northern Sea Route, raising U.S. concerns over the Polar Silk Road strategy.
articles.body: China is testing whether the top of the world can become a new strategic trade corridor, launching regular seasonal container service to Europe through Russia’s Arctic as Beijing and Moscow deepen their commercial and military footprint in a region Washington increasingly views as critical to U.S. security. The service remains limited in scale, with just over eight voyages planned this season, but China analyst Gordon Chang told Fox News Digital that its significance goes beyond the number of containers currently making the journey. "China has a major strategic push on the Arctic for various reasons," Chang said in an interview. "Arctic ice is melting, and this means that the Northern Sea Route, which hugs Russia's north coast, does become viable at least for a few months in the summer." TRUMP ENVOY WARNS CHINA'S POWER MOVE AT SEA IS THREAT 'WE CANNOT AFFORD TO IGNORE' Sea Legend Shipping’s Dubai Tower departed Ningbo-Zhoushan Port on Aug. 15 for Europe via Russia’s Northern Sea Route, with the journey to Felixstowe, England, scheduled to take about 20 days, according to China Daily on Aug. 17. The move comes as a new U.S. congressional commission staff report warns that Russia’s increasing isolation and dependence on Beijing are giving China greater leverage — including greater access to the Arctic. Chang warned that Washington needs a stronger physical presence in response. "We need to be in the Arctic, and President Trump has authorized more icebreakers," he told Fox News Digital. "We are woefully short in that department." TIM SHEEHY EXPOSES A 'SCARY' SHIPBUILDING COLLAPSE THAT LEAVES THE US VULNERABLE TO CHINA A White House official told Fox News Digital on background that, "The Arctic is a critical region for U.S. national security and the economy. As an Arctic nation, the United States will pursue its security and economic interests and ensure safety, stability, and prosperity in the face of growing competition from China and Russia." A fact sheet released Aug. 20 by staff of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and subsequent economic isolation from the West have "compelled Russia to accept a greater Chinese presence in the Arctic," a region Moscow has traditionally regarded as central to its sovereignty and national security. CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE The report said Chinese state-owned enterprises now hold a combined 20% stake in the U.S.- and EU-sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project, while China and Russia are developing year-round commercial shipping along the Northern Sea Route. The two countries have also established a joint venture to manufacture ice-class container vessels, with the first ship planned to enter service in 2027. The Pentagon’s 2024 Arctic Strategy similarly said changing climate conditions are increasing accessibility in the region while China seeks greater influence and access there. The strategy identified Beijing’s proposed "Polar Silk Road" as a vehicle for infrastructure and natural-resource investments in the Arctic and warned that growing cooperation between China and Russia could "‘alter the Arctic’s stability and threat picture.’" For China-Europe commerce, the Northern Sea Route offers a radically different path from the traditional westbound journey through the Strait of Malacca, Indian Ocean, Bab el-Mandeb, Red Sea and Suez Canal. "This of course avoids some choke points, like the Strait of Malacca, the Bab el-Mandeb, the Suez Canal, the Strait of Gibraltar," Chang said. "So this is important for China." The new USCC report argues that China is increasingly benefiting from an asymmetric relationship in which Moscow needs Beijing more than Beijing needs Moscow. It says China has become indispensable to Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, giving Beijing growing leverage to obtain discounted energy and greater access to Russian military technology while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance. Energy is a major part of that imbalance. According to the report, China accounts for roughly half of Russia’s crude oil exports, while Russian crude represents only about one-fifth of China’s oil imports. The report says China has purchased approximately $372 billion in Russian fossil fuels since the invasion of Ukraine. UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC Moscow is now making increasingly aggressive use of the same Arctic passage to move oil east. Reuters reported Aug. 11 that Russia had sent seven crude shipments totaling roughly 6 million barrels toward Asia through the Northern Sea Route so far this season, nearly half the amount transported during the entire 2025 season. China is the principal destination for those shipments, according to Reuters. The growing Arctic activity comes as Washington has become increasingly concerned about Chinese and Russian cooperation close to Alaska. Chang pointed to the Bering Strait — separating Russia from Alaska — as a strategic vulnerability even on the Arctic route. CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS "There is one choke point though, which is of interest," he said. articles.title: French becoming more effective in stopping small boat crossings, UK says
articles.summary: The Home Office credits France with intercepting hundreds of potential crossings this summer using new tactics.
articles.body:
French police tactics are becoming more effective in stopping small boats in the English Channel from reaching Britain, the Home Office has said.

It credits French authorities with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants this summer over four separate weeks, as well as stopping 12 boats at sea using new techniques.

Footage released by French police shows officers racing across a beach in jeeps to intercept a launch. Once the boat is abandoned, an officer slashes it lengthways with a knife.

The Conservatives described the announcement as a "joke" and said Channel crossing preventions were "down by half over the past year".

Migrants can be seen throwing objects at the officers, one of whom appears to respond with pepper spray.

While Channel crossings are down about 40% compared to last year, thousands of illegal migrants are getting through with 250 arriving on Monday.

In late July a record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat with Border Security Command pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on 23 July.

The Home Office, citing French police figures, said that since it struck a deal with France three months ago which included additional funding for authorities, 61% of small boats have been intercepted - a five per cent increase compared to last year.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the "UK-France deal is already having a real impact".

The UK-France Border Security deal agreed in April under the Starmer government, includes Â£501m over three years to strengthen operations in northern France and Â£161m for new approaches.

Previously the French authorities allowed most dinghies to head towards the UK once they had launched, because of the risk of intercepting them in deep water, while loaded with people.

Of the 12 dinghies stopped so far at sea, three interceptions took place in the last two weeks.

The techniques being used have not been disclosed by the UK or France.

Charlie Eastaugh, director of maritime and small boats at the Border Security Command, told the BBC that "last Thursday alone, the French prevented all three of the boats that tried to cross".

Speaking to the BBC at the Western Jetfoil facility in Dover used to process migrants, he said: "Two of those they prevented at sea, and one they prevented on land."

Between 1 January and 24 August 2026, a total of 15,897 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 44% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 42% of asylum applications between April 2025 to March 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 25 August 2025 to 24 August 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to âsmash the gangsâ behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from April 2025 to March 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,000 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,535 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from April 2025 to March 2026. This was down by 22% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

He said some had claimed bad weather was the biggest factor in a reduction of crossings this year.

"But what that demonstrates is absolutely that the French are being effective in preventing a number of these small boats."

"Clearly, every single day that one slips through the net and crosses, it's one too many, and that's why it's absolutely critical to us to not take our foot off the gas and to keep working hard with our French partners and stop this from happening."

In the last week, 425 migrants made it across the Channel on five boats during three days of good weather.

Stopping the trade in equipment for Channel crossings is the first layer of tactics being used by the UK and other countries.

Dinghies, outboard engines, and life preservers have been seized by police in Germany.

Nearer the coast, boats have been discovered buried on beaches and in cars heading for the coast.

With less equipment available, people smugglers have resorted to using bigger boats.

Earlier this month a "mega-dinghy", with 230 people on board , was intercepted in the Channel.

The second layer is to stop migrants launching from beaches.

In July last year a BBC team witnessed the police slashing an inflatable boat with a knife to prevent it being used. This technique is now being used more often.

Interception at sea is the most difficult challenge. The UK government knows if it can prevent migrant boats getting into British waters, where the Border Force is legally obliged to pick them up, the incentive to try to cross will be reduced.

The concern is that smuggling gangs will continue to adapt but Eastaugh told the BBC that changes to their methods demonstrated how hard they are finding it to operate.

"That's why the numbers we're seeing are so successful, and we're absolutely not complacent, and we must keep working this way to keep the numbers down," he said.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "The only way we can stop the crossings is by having a proper deterrent. If people know they can stay in the UK, get put up in a hotel and claim benefits then they will keep risking these dangerous journeys."

Earlier this month Reform UK said if it was in power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.

The French interior ministry responded by saying it would "constitute a violation of French sovereignty".

articles.title: Venezuelans, Cubans, Colombians arrive in African nation under Trump deportation deal
articles.summary: Deportees from Venezuela, Cuba, and Colombia arrived in Liberia as the West African nation agreed to accept up to 1,200 foreign nationals from the US over the next year.
articles.body: Authorities in Liberia received the country’s first deportation flight from the U.S. on Thursday under an agreement with Washington to accept up to 1,200 foreign nationals over the next year. The West African nation, which was expected to receive 20 deportees, received nationals mostly from Latin America, including Venezuela, Cuba and Colombia, Liberian Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah told Reuters. Many of the deportees were sent to Liberia to seek protection from being returned to their home countries, where judges determined they could face torture or other abuse, Liberian officials said. Liberia has said the arrivals reflect its longstanding role as a sanctuary for displaced people. Officials said the migrants will be "free to depart the country" when desired or apply for formal asylum. The deportees will also receive services from the International Organization for Migration and the U.N. refugee agency, officials said, Reuters reported. SOUTH AFRICA’S ILLEGAL MIGRATION BACKLASH MIRRORS POLITICAL BATTLES ACROSS THE WEST According to Reuters, the plane departed from Louisiana and stopped in Senegal before landing in Monrovia at 12:45 p.m. local time. In a statement Tuesday, Liberia highlighted its history of accepting people "seeking refuge from political and other crises" and said it will not repatriate anyone until legal proceedings are complete. "The Government of the Republic of Liberia agrees not to return any person transferred to Liberia by the Government of the United States of America to their home country or country of former habitual residence until a final decision has been made regarding any pending protection claims," officials said. "The Government wants to emphasize that those being brought to Liberia are not criminals and are not being prosecuted in any manner under United States or Liberian law. They are being received as guests of the Republic of Liberia," officials said. DHS TOUTS MILLIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT DEPARTURES AS BORDER CROSSINGS DROP 94% UNDER TRUMP Liberia said it is not demanding compensation under the deal but will receive "support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly." Reuters said the U.S. awarded Liberia $5 million this year for "migration management activities." Liberia’s agreement to accept up to 1,200 deportees makes it one of the largest such deals on the African continent. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The U.S. also reached agreements with several other African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, Ghana and Sierra Leone, Reuters said. Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Meta’s Zuckerberg buys 19th-century castle in southeast of Ireland
articles.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has bought a 19th-century Gothic-style castle in the southeast of Ireland, 125 miles from his company’s European headquarters.
articles.body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has bought a 19th-century Gothic-style castle overlooking a river in the southeast of Ireland, 125 miles from his company’s European headquarters, a spokesman said on Thursday. Strancally Castle was built around 1830 on land overlooking the River Blackwater and underwent extensive renovation in 2003, according to a state architectural archive. The transaction is not listed on the Irish state property price register. The Irish Times, which first reported the purchase, estimated the property might be worth between €20 million ($23.4 million) and €30 million ($35.1 million). A spokesman for Zuckerberg said he and his family were “excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland.” Meta employs around 1,500 people in Ireland, where a number of U.S. tech multinationals have their European headquarters, in part due to the country’s favorable tax regime.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's trial is playing out in court. Online, it's become something else.
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's trial has become a social media obsession, fueling discussion about postpartum mental health while spawning unsupported theories about her c...
articles.body:
The Lindsay Clancy trial is dominating headlines, but the public fascination with the 36-year-old Duxbury, Mass., woman who is accused of killing her three children in January 2023 — and whose defense argues she was experiencing postpartum psychosis at the time — goes beyond the typical true crime story.

The trial has also gone viral on social media, where users are eager to follow every new development, or do some armchair sleuthing of their own — sharing theories with their followers. The case has even prompted discussions around postpartum depression, symptoms of which are reported by roughly 1 in 8 women , and broader gaps in maternal mental health care.

Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children, but has pleaded not guilty , with her attorneys arguing that she was not criminally responsible due to mental illness. To convict her, prosecutors will have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that she was criminally responsible at the time of the killings.

The defense rested its case on Friday , and closing arguments could happen as early as Monday. As the trial nears its end, let's take a look at why this case has become social media fodder — for better or for worse.

Clancy, who worked as a labor and delivery nurse for nine years, married her husband, Patrick Clancy, in 2016, and had three children with him: Cora, 5 at the time of her death; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months. According to a medical malpractice lawsuit against some of her psychiatrists, which was filed earlier this year and features much of the same history of her medical treatment, she experienced postpartum anxiety after the birth of her first two children, which she managed with therapy and lifestyle changes like exercise .

But after Callan's birth, her symptoms grew more severe, she said, including extreme insomnia, anxiety and behavior that she described as manic. Lindsay sought help from mental health professionals, who prescribed her over a dozen medications, and even admitted herself into a psychiatric hospital weeks before the Jan. 24, 2023, deaths of her children. She was discharged after five days.

Lindsay is now paraplegic and uses a wheelchair after an apparent suicide attempt following the killings.

It's a shocking case. Neuropsychologist Sanam Hafeez tells Yahoo that's part of the reason the public can't look away. "As humans, we're gripped by horrible things," she explains. "It's like wanting to watch a car crash on the highway."

There's also a gendered element to Lindsay's case that seems to attract women in particular, Hafeez says. For one, it's a story about a mother on trial for the deaths of her three small children — a situation that many would view as unimaginable.

But Hafeez says that many people are also interested in Lindsay's life as a mom before the killings, noting that many women — particularly those struggling with motherhood — may be able to relate to aspects of her experience.

For example, some people online have accused Patrick of being an absent father . (According to People , he would often go on work trips, leaving Lindsay alone with the children.) Some accuse him of not taking Lindsay's mental health as seriously. Others have taken issue with his divorcing Lindsay and then remarrying more than three years after their children's deaths. Hafeez says many women are finding surprising kinship with the defendant, who they see as an example of a woman who may not have received proper support in her relationship.

In his trial testimony, Patrick defended his ex-wife as a " very dedicated " mother who did everything for them. He said he helped her seek treatment, including encouraging her to admit herself to the hospital, and said no medical provider ever told him not to leave Lindsay alone with their children. He'd left them with her before, he said, and nothing had happened.

"There's so much hatred and anger from every woman who's been jilted or ignored or disappointed by a man," Hafeez says. "I think a lot of the fascination comes from not just the psychosis and not what she did … it's the circumstances that led to this."

Another reason the case may resonate with people is because Lindsay repeatedly sought treatment for her mental health issues but continued to experience symptoms.

"I think for women, primarily for moms, there is a sense of heartbreak and validation," Nicole Kumi , a postpartum expert and founder of The Whole Mom , tells Yahoo. "Because a lot of us can see pieces of ourselves within Lindsay."

Lindsay Clancy's case is sparking broader discussions about postpartum mental health

Media coverage of Lindsay's case has inspired people to share their own postpartum experiences — many of which go undiscussed — with some saying they see aspects of their own experiences in her story and wondering what might have happened without proper intervention.

Kumi tells Yahoo that one of the positive effects of this case's virality is that it has prompted people to share crucial information with others.

"So many moms are sharing their stories and their journeys, and normalizing that it's OK to ask for help, that it is actually the best thing to do," she says. "They're also sharing who they got help from, and are linking their information. Providers are also coming out of our shells a little bit more, and speaking more about this topic and the work that we're doing — we are really starting to build a network."

Supporting mothers during pregnancy, as well as afterwards, can help prevent future tragedies, Kumi says, adding that the interest in the Clancy case suggests society is at an inflection point to make real change.

"What we have been asking for all along is education and better care — not just expecting moms to speak up when they're in crisis, but giving them tools and resources before the crisis," she says. "There's a real opportunity here for our country to make systemic changes that will impact generations to come."

Armchair sleuths are invested in the case. That could have an unintended consequence.

Lindsay's case has sparked intense debate over whether she should be held criminally responsible. But some armchair investigators have taken the case a step further, pointing to what they say are inconsistencies in the evidence. Some have even promoted baseless theories that Patrick could have been responsible for his children's deaths. Patrick has never been implicated in the case, and Lindsay's own defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, has not addressed these theories.

Kathryn Coduto , an assistant professor of media science at Boston University, tells Yahoo that these theories tend to spread online because, when it comes to true crime cases, "one of the hallmarks is that men are typically the perpetrators."

"So I think then, this case basically flipping that brings a lot of attention. It's not just a woman who is a perpetrator here, but it's a mother, and it's a mother who killed her kids, and they're young kids," she says.

Dominique Russo , a Florida-based criminal defense lawyer who has covered the Clancy case on TikTok , tells Yahoo that another reason these theories catch on is because much of the public's exposure to criminal trials is on TV.

"Most people in the public have not gone through a criminal trial before, and they're basing their knowledge on things like Law and Order: SVU that always has a twist," she says. "It's never the person that they start out thinking that it's going to be. There's always something that gets uncovered at the end of the day, and something that blows up the case."

The reason these conspiracy theories continue to gain traction, Russo says, is because "it doesn't make good content to be like, 'Oh no, it was just Lindsay and it's an insanity issue.'"

"People are getting views because they're breaking down the timeline, they're picking apart the evidence, and all of that," she explains. And, as Coduto notes, some social media users have all the time in the world to pick apart tiny pieces of evidence, without necessarily having context about what has been excluded from the trial and why.

But it is possible, Russo says, for social media to have an impact on how Lindsay's lawyer is trying this case. Ultimately, it's a jury of Lindsay's peers who will decide the outcome of the trial, she says, and the arguments resonating on social media may resonate with the jury as well.

paragraphs: The Lindsay Clancy trial is dominating headlines, but the public fascination with the 36-year-old Duxbury, Mass., woman who is accused of killing her three children in January 2023 — and whose defense argues she was experiencing postpartum psychosis at the time — goes beyond the typical true crime story.

The trial has also gone viral on social media, where users are eager to follow every new development, or do some armchair sleuthing of their own — sharing theories with their followers. The case has even prompted discussions around postpartum depression, symptoms of which are reported by roughly 1 in 8 women , and broader gaps in maternal mental health care.

Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children, but has pleaded not guilty , with her attorneys arguing that she was not criminally responsible due to mental illness. To convict her, prosecutors will have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that she was criminally responsible at the time of the killings.

The defense rested its case on Friday , and closing arguments could happen as early as Monday. As the trial nears its end, let's take a look at why this case has become social media fodder — for better or for worse.

Clancy, who worked as a labor and delivery nurse for nine years, married her husband, Patrick Clancy, in 2016, and had three children with him: Cora, 5 at the time of her death; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months. According to a medical malpractice lawsuit against some of her psychiatrists, which was filed earlier this year and features much of the same history of her medical treatment, she experienced postpartum anxiety after the birth of her first two children, which she managed with therapy and lifestyle changes like exercise .

But after Callan's birth, her symptoms grew more severe, she said, including extreme insomnia, anxiety and behavior that she described as manic. Lindsay sought help from mental health professionals, who prescribed her over a dozen medications, and even admitted herself into a psychiatric hospital weeks before the Jan. 24, 2023, deaths of her children. She was discharged after five days.
Lindsay is now paraplegic and uses a wheelchair after an apparent suicide attempt following the killings.

It's a shocking case. Neuropsychologist Sanam Hafeez tells Yahoo that's part of the reason the public can't look away. "As humans, we're gripped by horrible things," she explains. "It's like wanting to watch a car crash on the highway."

There's also a gendered element to Lindsay's case that seems to attract women in particular, Hafeez says. For one, it's a story about a mother on trial for the deaths of her three small children — a situation that many would view as unimaginable.

But Hafeez says that many people are also interested in Lindsay's life as a mom before the killings, noting that many women — particularly those struggling with motherhood — may be able to relate to aspects of her experience.

For example, some people online have accused Patrick of being an absent father . (According to People , he would often go on work trips, leaving Lindsay alone with the children.) Some accuse him of not taking Lindsay's mental health as seriously. Others have taken issue with his divorcing Lindsay and then remarrying more than three years after their children's deaths. Hafeez says many women are finding surprising kinship with the defendant, who they see as an example of a woman who may not have received proper support in her relationship.

In his trial testimony, Patrick defended his ex-wife as a " very dedicated " mother who did everything for them. He said he helped her seek treatment, including encouraging her to admit herself to the hospital, and said no medical provider ever told him not to leave Lindsay alone with their children. He'd left them with her before, he said, and nothing had happened.

"There's so much hatred and anger from every woman who's been jilted or ignored or disappointed by a man," Hafeez says. "I think a lot of the fascination comes from not just the psychosis and not what she did … it's the circumstances that led to this."
Another reason the case may resonate with people is because Lindsay repeatedly sought treatment for her mental health issues but continued to experience symptoms.

"I think for women, primarily for moms, there is a sense of heartbreak and validation," Nicole Kumi , a postpartum expert and founder of The Whole Mom , tells Yahoo. "Because a lot of us can see pieces of ourselves within Lindsay."
Lindsay Clancy's case is sparking broader discussions about postpartum mental health

Media coverage of Lindsay's case has inspired people to share their own postpartum experiences — many of which go undiscussed — with some saying they see aspects of their own experiences in her story and wondering what might have happened without proper intervention.
Kumi tells Yahoo that one of the positive effects of this case's virality is that it has prompted people to share crucial information with others.

"So many moms are sharing their stories and their journeys, and normalizing that it's OK to ask for help, that it is actually the best thing to do," she says. "They're also sharing who they got help from, and are linking their information. Providers are also coming out of our shells a little bit more, and speaking more about this topic and the work that we're doing — we are really starting to build a network."

Supporting mothers during pregnancy, as well as afterwards, can help prevent future tragedies, Kumi says, adding that the interest in the Clancy case suggests society is at an inflection point to make real change.

"What we have been asking for all along is education and better care — not just expecting moms to speak up when they're in crisis, but giving them tools and resources before the crisis," she says. "There's a real opportunity here for our country to make systemic changes that will impact generations to come."

articles.title: âIn contempt for gathering peopleâ: Pak blames ex PM Imran Khanâs party for hospital transfer
articles.summary: Pakistan News: NEW DELHI: The Pakistan government on Saturday blamed jailed former prime minister Imran Khanâs Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Pakistan government on Saturday blamed jailed former prime minister Imran Khanâs Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital instead of the private facility ordered by the Supreme Court for his medical checkup.Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) after a large number of PTI workers gathered outside Shifa International Hospital.The development came after Khanâs sister, Uzma Khan, approached the Supreme Court alleging that the government and senior officials had violated its order to shift the former prime minister to the private hospital.The Supreme Court had on August 18 directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa Hospital within two days and keep him there until the next hearing on September 16. Instead, Khan was taken to PIMS and later returned to jail after doctors declared him fit.Govt says court order was followedTarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content, leaving authorities with no option but to shift Khan elsewhere.âContempt has definitely happened,â Tarar said, accusing Khanâs sister and PTI of violating the courtâs directions by turning the medical checkup into a political issue.The minister maintained that the government had implemented the Supreme Courtâs order âin letter and spiritâ. He said the medical examination was conducted transparently, Khanâs sister was present and doctors from Shifa Hospital were involved in the process.The Supreme Courtâs order followed months of concerns raised by Khanâs family and supporters over his health, particularly an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year. Khan was taken to PIMS several times after being diagnosed with right central retinal vein occlusion in late January.A report submitted by jail authorities to the Supreme Court said his eye condition had improved significantly and that his vision was âalmost normalâ.Khan has been lodged in Rawalpindiâs Adiala Jail since 2023 in connection with several cases.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: NSA Doval to visit Beijing for 25th round of India-China border talks
articles.summary: India News: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval is set to arrive in Beijing on Monday for the 25th round of India-China Special Representatives talks on the boun.
articles.body: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval is set to arrive in Beijing on Monday for the 25th round of India-China Special Representatives talks on the boundary issue with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.The talks are scheduled to take place on Tuesday, according to official sources, as cited by PTI.The talks come ahead of the expected visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12-13.While Beijing has not officially confirmed Xiâs participation, officials on both sides remain optimistic that he will attend, potentially opening the way for a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi to discuss steps to advance bilateral ties.Doval and Wang serve as the designated Special Representatives for the boundary talks mechanism, established in 2003 to seek a comprehensive resolution to the India-China border dispute, which stretches 3,488 km.Although the mechanism has not resolved the boundary dispute, officials on both sides consider it a useful platform for managing recurring tensions and addressing differences between the two countries.Doval and Wang last met in August 2025 on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin.Ahead of the upcoming talks in Beijing, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday reiterated that peace and tranquillity along the border are essential for maintaining good relations between India and China.External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said earlier this month that India views issues concerning the border areas with China as âmost seriousâ and stressed that maintaining peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) is of âutmost importanceâ. He said the situation along the frontier would determine the overall trajectory of India-China relations.New Delhi had earlier rejected Beijingâs criticism of Indiaâs decision to assign official names to 27 places and geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh, asserting that the state is an âinalienable and integralâ part of India and that nothing can change this âindisputable realityâ.China, which claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of South Tibet, has issued its own set of names for places in the region since 2017.India has dismissed the practice as âvain and preposterousâ, maintaining that such actions cannot alter the âundeniableâ reality that Arunachal Pradesh âwas, is, and willâ always remain an integral part of India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1995, a retired British bus driver began covering his modest home with empty beer containers; around 75,000 cans later, it was known as the Can House
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the story of the Can House in Hartlepool, a unique folk art site created by Philip Muspratt using 75,000 beer cans. Explore its history, impact on the community, and legacy after its demolition.
articles.body: What began as an unremarkable project became the Can House, one of Englandâs most unusual folk art sites, in Hartlepool. Philip Muspratt was born in 1952 and passed away in 2015. Between his birth and death, he served in the armed forces as well as being employed as a bus driver until his early retirement due to a disability, as recorded in the SPACES Archives entry on the Can House and noted in local obituaries describing him as a retired bus driver who died aged 63. The project began as a simple gesture of kindness, not as a work of art. This began when Muspratt decided to decorate his back garden with found materials to cheer his elderly father, who was deaf and unable to speak.The Can House, an entry from the SPACES Archives, a nonprofit organization that documents self-taught art environments, describes how the project's true starting point came when Muspratt noticed piles of empty beer bottles left behind by his son and his son's friends. So he decided to construct a wall from them in his back garden, a construction that reached two layers of bottles in width, five feet in height, and approximately 23 feet in length, which took him five months to build, as described in the SPACES Archives entry on the Can House. The same entry reports that Musprattâs son was struggling with alcoholism, giving him a steady supply of used bottles for the project.From bottles to cansThe project switched materials around 2005. After learning that his son had switched to drinking from cans, Muspratt began collecting cans instead. His hobby quickly became more serious: he aimed to keep decorating the property with empties and raise money to restore a local war memorial through scrap metal sales. People around Muspratt heard about the project and began sending him bags of empty cans.A landmark and a filmThe Can House became more than just a curiosity for one individual. It attracted visitors from outside Hartlepool, including some from America, and became a social hub after many nearby pubs had closed. RIP the Can House, a Cultural Landmark Made from Empty Beer Cans, a retrospective published by Vice, describes how filmmaker Maxy Bianco spent time documenting life inside the house for a 52âminute film first screened in 2012 and later shared online, which drew more than 20,000 views and a screening at Londonâs Floating Cinema in Hackney Wick. The Vice article notes that Muspratt had started covering the semiâdetached house in 2005, eventually layering on more than 75,000 beer cans in intricate patterns, including a fully functioning can fountain in the back garden. Biancoâs 52âminute documentary follows not just the house but Muspratt, his wife Sue, and their children and grandchildren, capturing both the communal drinking and the toll of daily alcohol abuse.The Vice story also sheds light on the complexities that were involved in building this colorful home. Biancoâs documentary showed both the sense of community the project created and the reality of the alcohol addiction behind its materials. According to Kevin McGrother, a local musician who recorded a video inside the house, Muspratt initially started to collect the cans to pay for the renovation of the memorial at the church, as quoted in Viceâs retrospective âRIP the Can House, a Cultural Landmark Made from Empty Beer Cans.End of the Can HouseMuspratt died in 2015, leaving the house deserted for several years after nearly two decades of decoration. The property was demolished as part of a larger redevelopment plan for Hartlepoolâs Dyke House area. The housing association Thirteen acquired the house as part of the Willow Fields redevelopment, which aimed to replace several prewar houses with 64 two- and three-bedroom homes. The demolition process started in 2018, and the entire house was torn down later that year, as reported in local news coverage of the Can Houseâs removal. Although the structure no longer stands, the Can House remains a notable example of vernacular art in Hartlepool. It joins other self-made art environments created by people without formal art training and reflects the roles of grief, addiction, and community in the project.Such details have since led to the site being recorded by archives and outsider art scholars as an extraordinary beer-can landscape within Western Europe: 75,000-odd cans neatly structured across facade and yard. In this instance, one of the SPACES Archives entries has the Can House listed with a host of other vernacular art environments; an example of how Muspratt converted a humble semi to an informally visited local landmark. And although the structure can no longer be visited, traces of its post-industrial creative spark survive in a wealth of photographs, news clippings and video shorts still appearing online.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Today’s leftists are dangerously wrong about communism. Just listen to the survivors
articles.summary: Survivors of communist regimes from Cuba, Venezuela, the Soviet Union and China shared firsthand stories of torture, empty shelves and lost freedom.
articles.body: When Americans defend free markets, they analyze real-world outcomes and quote economists. When radicals defend communism, they ignore history and those who experienced it firsthand. The omissions are deliberate. Survivors of communist regimes are dangerous to the argument because they are proof of its outcome. They know what happens after the government acquires the power it promised to use only for the public good. I recently gathered survivors of communist regimes in the Capitol to hear their stories. They came from Cuba, Venezuela, the Soviet Union and China. One endured torture in prison. Another watched grocery shelves empty as his community decayed. Others saw schools converted into instruments of indoctrination and churches treated as enemies of the state. THE MEN WHO FLED THESE SOCIALIST REGIMES HAVE A TERRIFYING WARNING José Daniel Ferrer spent more than 12 years in Cuban prisons. He endured physical and psychological torture, and watched fellow citizens die from the same abuse and malnutrition he experienced. He understands the deception communists employ that made those prisons possible. "It’s the best evidence that the communists who try to get to power in democratic nations are scam artists," Ferrer said. "Fidel Castro and Hugo Chávez denied what they were until they had secured power." RNC WARNS DEMOCRATS FACE 'POLITICAL SUICIDE' AFTER DSA PRAISES FIDEL CASTRO, DEMANDS RUBIO'S PROSECUTION Castro denied being a communist before consolidating power for himself. Chávez sold himself as a democratic reformer before turning Venezuela into an authoritarian state. The radical label is hidden while votes are needed, then embraced once the institutions capable of restraining them have been weakened. We see the same deception among American politicians who call themselves "Democratic Socialists." They insist the label separates them from communism while embracing the concentration of economic and political power that has defined every communist movement. DEMOCRATS' SOCIALIST SURGE PROVES AMERICA'S 250-YEAR FIGHT FOR FREEDOM ISN'T OVER Communism’s advocates respond to witnesses like Ferrer by reaching for an excuse. They blame sanctions, corruption, foreign interference or the supposed betrayal of an otherwise noble idea. Their theory is always innocent. The people who suffered under it are somehow mistaken about what happened to them. Daniel Di Martino’s family suffered from the same communist deception in Venezuela. Before the Bolivarian Revolution, they had an apartment, steady work, and an ordinary middle-class life. Then the promises were replaced by empty shelves and government rationing. Milk disappeared from stores. Meat became scarce. The government assigned citizens shopping days and required them to scan their fingerprints before determining what they were allowed to purchase. This is how communist control enters daily life. It doesn’t always begin with soldiers in the streets. Sometimes, it’s just a few regulations at the grocery store. SOCIALISM WILL 'CONTROL PEOPLE' AND 'TAKE EVERYTHING AWAY' FROM AMERICA, ACCORDING TO THESE EXPATS "The common denominator is that they destroy free enterprise," Di Martino said. "You cannot start a business, you cannot feed your family, therefore you die, or you flee." When the state controls food, employment and housing, citizens lose the ability to provide for themselves without bureaucrats' permission. The government does not need to imprison every dissident. It can seize your paycheck, apartment or your next meal. People who depend on the state for sustenance live at the will and convenience of their captor. SEN TOM COTTON: DEMOCRATS SAY SOCIALISM WILL HELP. HISTORY SAYS IT WILL HURT Communism doesn’t just control your physical necessities. Mike Gonzalez shared how it wages war on faith, conscience and independent thought. As a child in Cuba in the 1970s, he was harassed for attending church and pressured to join the communist Pioneers. Regime thugs interrogated him at age 11. Communism’s advocates respond to witnesses like Ferrer by reaching for an excuse. They blame sanctions, corruption, foreign interference or the supposed betrayal of an otherwise noble idea. Their theory is always innocent. The people who suffered under it are somehow mistaken about what happened to them. "Why did communists try to control the schools and didn’t like church?" he asked. "Because they tried to control the message." EXPERT WHO FLED CUBA WARNS OF ‘VICIOUS CYCLE’ THAT WILL LEAD TO ‘COMMUNISTS IN DOUBLE DIGITS’ IN CONGRESS Faith, family and national traditions remind people that the state is neither the source of truth nor the highest object of devotion. articles.title: Ukraine drone attack kills 2 children in Russiaâs Krasnodar, sets logistics hub ablaze
articles.summary: Europe News: Two children were killed and nine others, including seven children, were injured after drone debris struck a private childcare centre in Krasnodar in .
articles.body: Two children were killed and nine others, including seven children, were injured after drone debris struck a private childcare centre in Krasnodar in southern Russia overnight, regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev said on Monday.The attack also damaged apartment buildings and triggered fires at warehouses in the city, Kondratyev said on Telegram. Russian online retailer Ozon separately said a fire broke out at one of its logistics hubs following the attack.The incident came as Ukraine stepped up strikes on Russian logistics and industrial facilities, while Russian forces continued attacks on Ukrainian cities.Three killed in Kharkiv attackIn Ukraine, a Russian attack on the outskirts of the northeastern city of Kharkiv killed three people, the regional governor said on Telegram late on Sunday.Ukraine has been seeking additional interceptor missiles from the United States and Europe as it tries to strengthen its air defences against Russian attacks, now in the fifth year of the war.The latest Russian and Ukrainian strikes come as both sides continue targeting infrastructure and military-related facilities far from the front lines.Drone attack repelled in StavropolIn Nevinnomyssk, an industrial area in Russia's Stavropol region near Krasnodar, authorities said a drone attack was repelled early Monday.Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said the attack targeted an industrial area in the city, which has a major chemical production sector.Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian logistics hubs and warehouses, bringing the impact of the war closer to civilians and businesses involved in the country's online retail economy.The strikes have also drawn a warning from Russian President Vladimir Putin. In comments published on Saturday, Putin said Kyiv had opened a "Pandora's box" by attacking Russian economic targets and warned that Moscow would target Ukraine's "most sensitive economic sectors".Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A British artist collected more than 100,000 plastic bottles and built an artificial island with a house, ponds and a waterfall
articles.summary: UK News: British artist Richart Sowa spent years collecting plastic bottles for a project most people would never attempt: building an entire island to live on.
articles.body: British artist Richart Sowa spent years collecting plastic bottles for a project most people would never attempt: building an entire island to live on. The result, called Joyxee Island, floated roughly 30 yards off the coast of Isla Mujeres, a small island off Mexico's Caribbean coast, with its base built from nets stuffed with more than 100,000 plastic bottles. On top of that floating foundation, Sowa built a genuinely functional home, complete with a solar-powered electrical system, a washing machine driven by wave motion, 2 swimming ponds, a waterfall and even an internet connection. He lived there with his wife and dog inside a 3-story house, an achievement that made Joyxee one of the more unusual owner-built homes anywhere in the world, and one built almost entirely from material most people simply throw away. The unusual project also attracted international attention, drawing curious visitors eager to see how discarded household waste could be transformed into a floating home. This remarkable feat of ingenuity demonstrates how creative determination can transform discarded materials into genuinely functional architecture, even when the elements ultimately prove too powerful to withstand.How Richart Sowa built Joyxee Island after losing his first bottle island to a hurricaneJoyxee was not Sowa's first attempt at building a home out of plastic bottles. His original project, called Spiral Island, was built in 1998 in a lagoon near Puerto Aventuras, after Sowa went through a period of soul-searching following the end of his first marriage and decided that living on a floating bottle island was genuinely what he wanted for his life. He stayed there with his 2 dogs until 2005, when Hurricane Emily destroyed the island entirely. Rather than abandon the idea, Sowa spent the following years collecting a fresh supply of bottles and began construction on Joyxee Island in late 2007, finishing the project by the end of 2008.What living on an 8,000-square-foot island made of recycled bottles actually looked likeOnce finished, Joyxee Island covered roughly 8,000 square feet and opened for public tours, with visitors able to reach the island using an 8-person barge Sowa had also built out of recycled bottles. Sowa designed the island with genuine self-sufficiency in mind, growing his own vegetables and herbs on site rather than treating the project purely as an art installation. The combination of solar power, wave-powered laundry and homegrown food meant the island functioned as an actual working household rather than a novelty structure, a detail that set Joyxee apart from many other bottle-based art projects that exist mainly to be photographed rather than lived in.Why Joyxee Island no longer exists todayJoyxee Island's story did not end the way Sowa likely hoped. According to Atlas Obscura, the island was damaged by storms in the years after it opened, and local authorities eventually required Sowa to remove it entirely, with the site confirmed gone as of a January 2019 update. Joyxee now exists only as a documented piece of history rather than a place visitors can still travel to, joining a small category of ambitious, owner-built structures that succumbed to the same coastal weather conditions that made their original construction so unusual in the first place. Sowa's 2 attempts at building a livable island out of plastic bottles remain a striking example of turning ordinary waste into genuine architecture, even if neither structure ultimately survived the Caribbean's storm season for good.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pay â¬25,000 for Schengen visa: Indian company BLS under probe after Spain's Algerian migration crisis
articles.summary: Europe News: Indian company BLS International has been drawn into a Spanish National Court investigation with links to alleged visa fraud network at Spainâs consul.
articles.body: Indian company BLS International has been drawn into a Spanish National Court investigation with links to alleged visa fraud network at Spainâs consulate in Algiers. The allegations have been denied by the firm.The probe, led by Judge MarÃ­a TardÃ³n, was expanded to examine the role of companies handling visa appointments and document processing, including BLS, which is contracted by Spainâs Foreign Ministry, as reported by Spanish news outlet The Objective.However, BLS International issued a statement rejecting any involvement in the alleged irregularities. "There is no evidence establishing any wrongdoing by BLS International or its employees in relation to the issuance of visas. BLS Internationalâs role is strictly administrative and is carried out in accordance with the requirements prescribed by the competent authorities," said the firm."All decisions relating to the processing and issuance or refusal of visas rest solely with the relevant diplomatic and consular authorities. BLS International remains committed to the highest standards of integrity, transparency, compliance and service delivery, and to its role as a trusted service partner to governments and citizens across the world," it added.The investigation began following âofficial communicationsâ from the Spanish Embassy in Algeria, which alerted authorities to a network allegedly âprofiting through the fraudulent issuance of Schengen visasâ. Judicial sources said the network allegedly charged applicants up to â¬25,000 per family to secure visas and residence or work permits, including for people who did not meet the formal requirements.The case initially led to the arrests of consulate chancellor Vicente Moreno and local employee Mohamed Boutouchent in April. Moreno's wife was also placed under investigation.Investigators allege Spanish officials and Algerian staff worked with outside companies involved in appointment scheduling and document management to prioritise applicants who paid bribes. The alleged network is accused of using unverified, altered or falsified documents to facilitate migration to Spain and, in some cases, secure residency in Spain or France.The judge is investigating five reported offences: money laundering, crimes against the rights of foreign citizens, repeated document falsification by a public official, influence peddling and membership in a criminal organisation. Investigators also claim that cash bribes were later laundered in Spain, including through vehicle purchases.Why BLS is under scrutinyThe court has specifically referred to âprocessing platforms like BLSâ as part of its investigation into collaborating companies. BLS was awarded a â¬175 million Spanish Foreign Ministry contract in 2016 to manage visa appointments and document processing at certain consulates. The company had taken over work previously handled by another Indian firm, VFS Global.The investigation is also examining whether such service providers helped create or process applications for applicants who paid the alleged bribes, while legitimate applicants were denied or bypassed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: I have eight kids. Here's why the 'back-to-school' mom memes break my heart
articles.summary: A mom of eight shares why back-to-school memes celebrating kids leaving may send the wrong message to children who notice more than we think.
articles.body: Summer is the best season. My kids have no school commitments and our time is spent getting together with friends, doing weekend trips, camping, going to the lake, and enjoying the time we have with each other. My oldest is already in college so I know the feeling of time slipping through my fingers as my kids get older and create lives of their own. Time with my husband and eight children is my most precious gift and while back-to-school season is exciting, it’s certainly bittersweet. The joy of watching my kids grow into the next stage of life is balanced out by the feeling that most of August is the Sunday before school starts. Raising kids is hard, and it’s okay to feel a little relief when structure returns. But I think we should be thoughtful about the message our children receive in the way we celebrate. JO FROST CALLS OUT MODERN PARENTING MISTAKES SHE SAYS ARE ROBBING CHILDREN OF BASIC LIFE SKILLS Scrolling through social media this time of year brings meme after meme of parents, usually moms, who are thrilled the school year is starting because it’s time to ship their kids off to someone else five days a week. The photos of moms in robes on their doorstep holding a glass of wine are everywhere. Kids notice when we seem overly eager to send them away. They remember whether we treated their presence as a burden or a gift. They hear how their parents are elated about sending them elsewhere for hours every day. Kids are much more perceptive than we give them credit for. Even if all of the back-to-school jubilation is in jest, deep down they know they are of some undue burden to their parents. NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD Conflicting emotions are common and parents shouldn’t beat themselves up over them. A study of 2,000 parents over the summer revealed 57% were happy about their kids returning to school but also felt guilty about it. Yet a different study showed 67% of parents who thought summer break was too long. I get that parents need a break, especially from the endless snack requests and demands of kids over the summer. No parent should be shamed for taking care of themselves in order to be a better parent for their kids. Yet that’s not what back-to-school season has become. It’s become a time when parents can thrillingly announce to the world that they are so happy to dump their kids at school and make them someone else’s problem. WHO IS RAISING AMERICA'S CHILDREN? MENTOR WARNS KIDS ARE SEEKING ROLE MODELS ONLINE AS COMMUNITIES FADE In a culture that has so devalued the family and children, this isn’t a surprise but it is disheartening. I used to think these kinds of posts were funny until I really thought about it. We only have so much time with our kids until they move out, go to school, and have lives of their own. I’m proud to watch my kids begin a new school year. I’m excited for what they’ll learn and who they’ll become. But I’m also sad to see summer end because I love having them home. I love the memories, the slow mornings, the time together, and the little moments that pass far too quickly. Parenting is hard and no one could ever be prepared for it, no matter how many books they read or other parents they talk to. We have so much responsibility on our plates that it can easily be overwhelming. Humans will make decisions based on their priorities — that’s what it all comes down to. Faith, marriage, kids, work, and hobbies all vie for the top spot and we have to make hard decisions every day but if those priorities are in order, it will be much easier to choose the right thing. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION I’m not suggesting every parent homeschool or drop everything to spend 24 hours a day catering to their kids. I’m saying that our children are incredible gifts and we should not be so anxious to shove them out the door and on the school bus for eight hours a day for nine or ten months of the year. Get involved in your kid’s school. Coach their rec team. Invite their friends for a movie night or ice cream or pizza making party at your house. Go on a hike with your kids and their friends. Be present. Put your phone down. Ask questions. Say ‘yes’ more. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We only have one life. Our kids are only young once and they see everything. I make plenty of mistakes as a mom but valuing the time I have with them is one mistake I try the hardest to avoid. So yes, celebrate back-to-school season. Just make sure your kids know they are loved, wanted, and deeply missed when they’re away.

articles.title: Salisbury artists create music and murals for River Park trail
articles.summary: The trail in Salisbury celebrates the history of the area and highlights local wildlife.
articles.body:
Artists have come together to create music and murals as part of a new nature trail.

The Salisbury River Park's Artwork Trail, in Wiltshire, has been created to celebrate the history of the area and highlight the local wildlife which calls the green space home.

Spots on the trail include fish-inspired picnic benches by local artist Zac Newham, a dragonfly sculpture by Jane Edden and drawings by illustrator Francesca McLean.

Clare Christopher, from Studio Response, which was involved in the project, said each artist brought "their own distinct voice" to the trail "while responding to the shared themes of nature, community and place that define the River Park".

'Alcohol ruled my life – now my eyes are open'

Historic windmill transformed with new sails

Fire that damaged allotments thought to be arson

The Salisbury River Park is a £45m green corridor of public open space which runs alongside the river Avon. It was built to deliver flood risk mitigation for the city.

Christopher added: "The trail offers a gentle, inviting way for people to experience the artworks, encouraging people to move through the River Park at their own pace, notice the details of the landscape and enjoy the artworks in relation to the river environment around them."

A trail map has been created which links each piece of art, with a version available for children.

Other artwork includes a mural by Fred Fieber on the coach park toilet block and Tech Moon's mural on the central car park toilet block which celebrates animals that can be found in the area including Atlantic Salmon and European Otter.

Composer Karen Wimhurst has contributed eight musical pieces inspired by the River Park and the neighbouring Avon Valley Nature Reserve, which can be listened to along the trail.

The project was curated by public art commissioning organisation Studio Response, in partnership with Salisbury City Council. The map has been released by the Environment Agency (EA).

Andy Wallis, Salisbury River Park project lead at the EA, said the trail was created to "reconnect people with the rivers that flow through their city."

He added: "Each piece encourages visitors to look more closely at the wildlife and natural heritage found along our chalk streams, from the delicate wings of a mayfly to the otters and kingfishers that call this place home."

articles.title: In 1998, Costa Rica spread 12,000 tonnes of orange waste over degraded pasture; 16 years later, tree diversity had tripled and forest biomass was 176% higher
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In the late 1990s, an unusual conservation experiment began in Costa Rica when ecologists proposed using orange peels and pulp to help restore a badly.
articles.body: In the late 1990s, an unusual conservation experiment began in Costa Rica when ecologists proposed using orange peels and pulp to help restore a badly degraded piece of land inside a national park.For this, orange juice company Del Oro and ecologists Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs, worked with the Area de Conservacion Guanacaste (ACG), or Guanacaste Conservation Area. According to Princeton University, the company had recently started production near the northern border of the conservation area and was looking for a way to deal with its orange waste.Janzen and Hallwachs proposed a deal wherein Del Oro would donate some of its forested land to the ACG. In return, the company could take its orange peel waste to a degraded pasture inside the park, where it could break down naturally.After the agreement was signed, around 1,000 truckloads of orange peels and pulp, totalling about 12,000 metric tonnes, were spread across the degraded land.Over the next several years, the area changed dramatically. A place that had once been covered by exposed rock and dead grass became a dense forest filled with trees, vines and other vegetation.A forest emergesThe site was largely forgotten after the orange waste was deposited. A rival orange juice company, TicoFruit, later sued Del Oro, arguing that the company had defiled a national park. The case reached Costa Ricaâs Supreme Court, which ruled in favour of TicoFruit.The legal dispute meant that the site received little attention for about 15 years. That changed in 2013, when Princeton University researcher Timothy Treuer was discussing possible research projects with Janzen.Janzen mentioned the orange-peel site to Treuer and said that although taxonomists had visited the area, it had not received a thorough evaluation. Treuer decided to visit it during another research trip to Costa Rica.When he arrived, the site looked completely different from what he expected. The vegetation had grown so densely that Treuer could not initially see the large sign marking the experiment.âIt was so completely overgrown with trees and vines that I couldnât even see the 7-foot-long sign with bright yellow lettering marking the site that was only a few feet from the road,â Treuer said, as quoted by Princeton.The contrast became even clearer when Treuer compared the orange-peel site with the nearby untreated pasture. The treated area had become a thick forest, while the neighbouring land remained much more open.âIt was just hard to believe that the only difference between the two areas was a bunch of orange peels. They look like completely different ecosystems,â Treuer explained.Researchers assess forestTreuer worked with Jonathan Choi, then a Princeton student studying ecology and evolutionary biology. The researchers compared the area treated with orange waste with a nearby untreated pasture. They also collected and analysed soil samples from both sites to determine whether the orange waste had changed the soil over time.They also measured vegetation in both areas. The team established 100-metre-long lines, known as transects, through the forest. Trees growing within three metres of these lines were measured and identified. The same approach was used in the untreated pasture across the road.The differences were substantial. The soil in the orange-waste area was richer in nutrients. The area also had greater tree biomass, more tree species and a more closed forest canopy.The study found a 176% increase in aboveground biomass within the three-hectare area that was examined. Aboveground biomass refers to the wood and other plant material growing above the soil, including the trees.The researchers also found a major difference in tree diversity. While the surrounding areas were dominated by one type of tree, the former orange-waste site had about two dozen species of vegetation.Wildlife returned to restored areaThe changes were not limited to plants. Researchers also found signs of a more developed ecosystem at the site. Among the discoveries was a tayra, a dog-sized mammal related to weasels, Diario AS reported. The researchers also found a huge fig tree that had grown in the area.Jonathan Choi described the site as even more impressive in person than he had expected. âWhile I would walk over exposed rock and dead grass in the nearby fields, Iâd have to climb through undergrowth and cut paths through walls of vines in the orange peel site itself.âThe size of the fig tree was another indication of how much the area had changed. Choi said the tree was about three feet in diameter and described it as massive. âYou could have had 20 people climbing in that tree at once and it would have supported the weight no problem. That thing was massive,â he said.The researchers published their findings in the journal Restoration Ecology in a paper titled âLow-Cost Agricultural Waste Accelerates Tropical Forest Regenerationâ.Timothy Treuer said the experiment was unusual because it showed that forest restoration and waste management could potentially work together. âThis is one of the only instances Iâve ever heard of where you can have cost-negative carbon sequestration,â Treuer said. âItâs not just a win-win between the company and the local park; itâs a win for everyone.âThe researchers, however, did not suggest that companies should simply take their waste and dump it in natural areas. Treuer specifically warned against such an approach. âWe donât want companies to go out there willy-nilly just dumping their waste all over the place,â Treuer said. âBut if itâs scientifically driven and restorationists are involved in addition to companies, this is something I think has really high potential.âCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: As Ukraine’s allies gather for big anniversary, one key backer is absent
articles.summary: The lack of visible senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
articles.body: Leaders of Ukraine’s international allies on Monday marked 35 years since the country broke away from the Soviet Union to become an independent nation. The U.K.’s Andy Burnham flew in, while France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz joined a call to reaffirm commitments to Kyiv. But senior officials from one longtime backer were notably absent from the public show of support: the United States. While U.S. senators and former officials visited Ukraine ahead of the commemorations, the apparent lack of senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine. The message sent was especially pointed as Monday also marks 4 1/2 years since President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Russia’s much smaller neighbor. Negotiations to reach a peace deal, which President Donald Trump once promised to achieve within 24 hours, have stalled as supplies of U.S. air defense missiles dwindle and the Russian leader ramps up threats to Ukraine’s allies. Britain’s Burnham was the highest-profile Western leader to fly in and co-chair a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of countries backing Ukraine. European Council President António Costa, as well as the heads of nearly a dozen European nations, was also in Kyiv, despite the country’s air force reporting Russian rocket and drone strikes overnight. Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukraine in a statement. “The United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work to support a negotiated settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war that establishes a lasting and durable peace,” it said. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked Rubio for “thoughtful” greetings, adding, “We will be glad to welcome you in Kyiv.” Over the weekend, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and James Lankford, R-Okla., met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Blumenthal attended a ceremony Monday. Former Vice President Mike Pence and ex-special envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg were also in Kyiv for meetings. Kellogg was considered “too close to Ukraine” by Russian negotiators before he stepped down in December, NBC News reported last year. Late Monday, a State Department spokesperson told NBC News that the newly arrived Chargé d’Affaires, Paul Houston, had attended official commemorations. In response to questions sent to the White House about the lack of senior administration representation at the events, a U.S. official said: “President Trump’s representatives speak with Ukrainian officials almost daily, and the United States has done more than anyone to bring this bitter war to an end.” On Tuesday, Zelenskyy said he received “warm and heartening congratulations” from Trump. The U.S. was once Ukraine’s most important supporter, providing billions of dollars in military aid and sharing critical intelligence. But since Trump returned to the Oval Office in early 2025, significant new aid has ceased, with the U.S. selling weapons to Ukraine’s NATO partners to be transferred to Kyiv instead. An analysis of how American aid flows have changed by the Council on Foreign Relations, a nonpartisan U.S. think tank, showed that as of March this year, Congress has made available $195 billion in spending related to the war in Ukraine. Of the $195 billion, $164 billion came from five pieces of legislation, the last of which was passed in April 2024, according to the report. U.K. and French support In recent days, the U.K. and France announced they would share critical military technology to help Ukraine defend itself. Britain has agreed to allow European missile manufacturer MBDA to release classified information on British-made components used in the SCALP long-range cruise missile. With the information from the U.K., Ukraine will be able to establish local assembly lines to produce the missile, which shares British and French technology, according to Downing Street. Zelenskyy also said this weekend that France’s Macron has agreed to accelerate the delivery of the latest French equipment and missiles. The European Commission also approved a further $7.1 billion in financial aid for Ukraine on Monday to procure new defense systems, such as air defense, missiles, ammunition and radars. With Moscow firing larger volleys of high-speed rockets at Ukraine’s cities, the country is staring down a long and perilous winter as it runs out of critically important interceptors capable of taking down Russian ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has pleaded with the U.S., the main maker of the interceptors for the Patriot missile air defense systems, to send Kyiv more, but the Iran war has depleted supplies and left Washington rationing remaining stock. A severe shortage of interceptors combined with a harsh winter and Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid could force Kyiv to come to the negotiating table under unfavorable terms. This is not the message that Zelenskyy sought to transmit, however. “Ukraine absolutely wants peace, but it is not ready to simply surrender,” he said in a defiant speech Monday.
