paragraphs: Governments around the world are increasingly offering cash payments, tax breaks, housing subsidies and childcare support in an effort to persuade citizens to have more children as birth rates fall and populations age.

Declining birth rates can strain a country's economy because there aren't enough people being born to support the aging population. That means greater strains on social programs like Social Security and Medicare in the United States since more and more people are using the programs, but not enough people are paying into them. Declining birth rates are a global problem, and a growing number of countries are rolling out increasingly generous pro-family incentives, ranging from direct payments for newborns to years of childcare assistance.

Singapore has spent years expanding financial support for families as it grapples with one of the world's lowest fertility rates. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong recently announced a major expansion of family support measures, emphasizing that the government wants to provide assistance well beyond a child's birth and into the early years of parenting.

Each child will receive almost S$70,000, the equivalent of about $55,000 USD, in direct financial support by the time they turn 17. The program will replace the current program, which includes the Baby Bonus Scheme.

Under the Baby Bonus Scheme, parents are given cash gifts throughout the first six-and-a-half years of a child's life. The first and second child get a total of S$11,000, equivalent to about $8,660 USD, disbursed in six-month increments, and every other child gets S$13,000, equivalent to about $10,236 USD.

Under the Large Families Scheme, which will also be replaced when the new package goes into effect, families can receive an additional $16,000 for each third or subsequent child born after February 18, 2025.
Despite those efforts, Singapore's birth rate remains among the lowest globally. The cash incentives began in 2001 and haven't been able to reverse the declining trend in birth rates.

"Ultimately, the decision to have children is a deeply personal one. Policies alone cannot make this happen. But what we can do is make it easier for Singaporeans who want children to start and raise a family," Wong said in a statement.
China has dramatically shifted from restricting births to actively encouraging them.

After decades of the one-child policy, Chinese officials are now trying to boost fertility as births have fallen and the population has begun shrinking. In 2025, Beijing rolled out a nationwide childcare subsidy that provides families with 3,600 yuan, or about $500, annually for each child under age three.

The subsidy is part of a broader campaign to encourage childbirth and ease the cost of raising children. Chinese authorities have also supported local initiatives that offer even larger payments, including monthly stipends and bonuses for families with multiple children.

"International practices show that cash subsidies are an indispensable part of pro-birth measures," Zhang Benbo, a researcher at a think tank under the National Development and Reform Commission, said in a statement at the time.
The national program is expected to benefit millions of households each year and reflects mounting concern over China's aging population and shrinking workforce.
Japan has become one of the world's most prominent examples of a nation battling demographic decline.

The country's aging population and persistently low fertility rate have prompted officials to expand financial support for families. Government measures include monthly child allowances, a childbirth lump-sum grant that has been increased to 500,000 yen, equivalent to $3,139 USD, and expanded childcare services.

Japan is also launching new childcare and education support initiatives in 2026. These reforms aim to reduce the financial burden of raising children by expanding access to childcare regardless of employment status and broadening financial assistance for families. While unveiling a policy to promote people having kids in 2023, Children's Policies Minister Masanobu Ogura said the next few years are possibly "a last chance" for Japan to change the trajectory of its declining birth rate.

"While diverse views about marriage, childbirth and childrearing should be respected, we want to make a society where young generations can marry, have and raise children as they wish," Ogura said, according to the Associated Press. "The basic direction of our measures to tackle low births is to reverse the trend of declining births by supporting individuals' pursuit of happiness."
Officials have repeatedly said the country's future economic strength depends in part on stabilizing population trends.

South Korea has spent billions of dollars attempting to increase what has frequently been ranked as the world's lowest fertility rate. The government offers an extensive package of benefits that includes monthly allowances for parents, direct birth grants, childcare support, expanded parental leave and housing assistance.

South Korea launched a program in 2022 that gave mothers 2 million won, the equivalent of about $1,500 USD, when they gave birth and then an additional 700,000 won, equivalent to about $500 USD, each month until their child turns one. Then, parents get 350,000 won, equivalent to about $260 USD, per month until they turn 2.

A major South Korean company is also offering its employees incentives to have kids. The Lotte Group, a massive conglomerate, gives employees with three or more children a free 7-9 seat family vehicle, and housing group Booyoung offers employees a $75,000 bonus for each new child they have.

"Korea will face a crisis of national existence 20 years from now, including a decline in the economically productive population and a shortage of defense personnel to ensure national security and maintain order," Booyoung chairman Lee Joong Keun told CBS News in 2024.
South Korea is still struggling with its birth rate, but the number of babies born in South Korea increased in 2024, the first time in nine years.

Sweden doesn't pay a cash bonus for having kids, but provides parents with a monthly allowance depending on the number of children they have. Each eligible child is given 1,250 SEK, the equivalent of $132 USD, and families with two or more children are eligible for the Large Family Supplement.

Parents with two kids receive an additional 150 SEK per month, equivalent to $15 USD; three-child families get 730 SEK, equivalent to $77 USD; four-child households get 1,740 SEK per month, equivalent to $183 USD, and families with five or more children get an extra 1,250 SEK per month per child, equivalent to about $132 USD.
The country offers generous paid parental leave, subsidized childcare and income support designed to make balancing careers and family life easier.
Estonia has combined direct payments with broader family support programs aimed at encouraging larger families.

Parents receive childbirth allowances and other child-related benefits, with support increasing for households with multiple children. The country also offers paid parental leave and childcare policies that policymakers say help reduce the cost of raising children.

Families with one or two eligible children receive 80 euros per child per month, equivalent to $93 USD, and families with three or more eligible children receive 100 euros per child per month, equivalent to $116 USD. The payments are made to parents until children turn 19.

Estonia's family policy has long been cited internationally as an example of how financial assistance can be paired with social programs to support parents. Government officials have repeatedly emphasized that encouraging family formation requires both direct financial support and practical assistance.
Estonia's birth rate has been on the decline since 2021. The child allowance started in 1992.

Finland has adopted a combination of cash benefits and family support services to encourage child-rearing. One of the country's most famous family programs is the baby box, which provides new parents with essential supplies for newborns. Families can also receive financial assistance and monthly benefits.

Parents of eligible children receive monthly payments until the child turns 17. Families with one child receive 94.88 euros, equivalent to $110 USD, 104.84 euros for the second child, 133.79 euros for the third child, equivalent to $156.11 USD, 173.24 euros for the fourth child, equivalent to $202.15 USD, 192.69 Euros for the fifth child, equivalent to $224.84 USD.
Despite being family-friendly, Finland has one of the lowest birth rates among the Nordic countries.
"So we cannot really any longer say that it's our good family policies that explain good fertility in the Nordics," Anneli Miettinen, a research manager at Kela, told NPR in 2025.
The United Arab Emirates offers some of the most generous childbirth-related financial support programs available to citizens.

Emirati families can qualify for substantial financial assistance tied to childbirth, while lower-income households may also receive monthly child allowances. Additional benefits are available for larger families, including support related to housing and debt relief.
Depending on where a person lives, a UAE native citizen can receive up to AED 220,000, equivalent to about $60,000 USD, after the birth of their child.

One of the country's notable programs includes the NAFIS child allowance initiative, which provides monthly payments for eligible children. These policies are designed to reduce family expenses and encourage population growth among Emirati citizens. Families can get AED 600 per qualifying child each month, equivalent to $163 USD.
The benefits generally apply only to UAE nationals rather than expatriate residents, reflecting the government's focus on supporting citizen families.
Can Cash Incentives Reverse Falling Birth Rates?
While governments continue expanding family benefits, researchers remain divided on how much direct financial incentives can raise birth rates.

Studies have found that generous payments and childcare support can influence family planning decisions, particularly when combined with broader policies that reduce the long-term cost of raising children. Data show that it can cause an immediate bump, but often doesn't fix long-term population declines. As fertility rates remain below replacement levels across much of the developed world, policymakers are increasingly experimenting with new approaches.

articles.title: Worker jabbed with needle after Glasgow bin lorry fire
articles.summary: The fire happened on Oban Drive at about 11:30 and forced the refuse vehicle to dump its rubbish on the street.
articles.body:
A council worker has been jabbed with a needle while cleaning up rubbish following another bin lorry fire in Glasgow.

The fire happened in Wilton Court at about 11:30 and forced the refuse vehicle to dump its rubbish on the street. Discarded vapes were found among the waste.

GMB union convener Chris Mitchell said the worker was jabbed with the needle during the clean-up and was taken to hospital for a Hepatitis B injection as a precaution.

It is understood to be the ninth fire in a Glasgow bin lorry this year, with the council previously urging the public to recycle batteries and vapes properly.

The fire happened four hours into the refuse workers' shift.

Mitchell said: "The crew acted with professionalism and made sure the load was safely ejected on the street before causing further damage.

"The crew and the general public were not harmed."

He said he was awaiting details as to how the fire started but said it could have been "another lithium battery fire".

"We would like to thank the cleansing teams for cleaning the area up," he said.

"Unfortunately, during the cleaning process another accident occurred where a council worker was jagged by a hypodermic needle.

"I would encourage the wider public when disposing of lithium batteries or sharp items to dispose of them properly.

"I will make this clear: we are one fire away from serious harm or damage."

Two weeks ago a bin lorry caught fire in Glasgow's Jamaica Street , prompting the council to issue a warning over the dangers of throwing batteries in normal rubbish.

There was a similar fire involving a bin lorry in Edinburgh last month.

A spokesman for Glasgow City Council said: "Our staff raised the alarm of a fire within their vehicle this morning and followed the correct procedure by unloading the waste onto the street.

"A cause for the fire has still to be confirmed, but discarded vapes were found within the waste that was off-loaded.

"If a discarded vape is confirmed as the cause of the fire, this incident will again highlight the danger linked to disposing of batteries and vapes in general waste."

He said the quick response of the crew ensured they were unharmed and the risk of damage to the vehicle was minimised.

"But it is vital that we all take care to recycle batteries and vapes properly," he said.

"Batteries and vapes can be safely recycled at a wide range of shops or at any of our household waste recycling centres."

A spokesman for the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said it was alerted to the fire in a bin lorry on Wilton Court at 11:28 and sent two appliances to the scene.

He said one casualty was taken to hospital and crews left the scene at 13:04 after ensuring the area had been made safe.

articles.title: Dangerous debris washes ashore before beachgoer makes another troubling find
articles.summary: A Jersey Shore beachgoer says she found more needle plungers and drug paraphernalia the day after Manasquan Beach reopened following a syringe cleanup.
articles.body: A popular Jersey Shore beach reopened to swimmers after dozens of syringes washed ashore — only for a beachgoer to report finding more concerning debris along the sand the following day. The syringes and paraphernalia were discovered littered across the sands of Manasquan Beach in Manasquan, New Jersey, along the Jersey Shore, on Saturday. Officials at the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) said the debris included household waste, including syringes used for at-home insulin injections, according to local outlets. DANGEROUS WATER WARNINGS HIT TRENDY VACATION SPOT AFTER POWERFUL STORM POUNDS AREA Mayor Michael Mangan told Fox News Digital the syringes were first discovered Saturday afternoon and were cleaned up and properly cleared away.  "There was a large amount of additional debris, indicating a garbage spill of some kind, and the incident was localized to the south end beach, along the Manasquan Inlet jetty," Mangan said. It's believed the debris washed ashore following recent heavy rainfall and sewer overflows, according to local reports citing the NJDEP. Mangan added that, in accordance with guidance from the NJDEP and Monmouth County health officials, the town waited for two high-tide cycles, which occurred overnight Saturday. SUMMER TRAVELERS WARNED AFTER FECAL BACTERIA LEVELS IN WATER EXCEED SAFETY STANDARDS By 9 a.m. Sunday, state and local officials "met on site, and no syringes were observed — so the water was reopened," Mangan told Fox News Digital. But not all residents agreed with the timing of reopening the waters. Priscilla Mahajan, a Manasquan resident, told local outlet News 12 she found needle plungers and drug paraphernalia on Sunday. Mahajan had participated in the cleanup efforts the day before. She said she felt the beach reopened too soon. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "One beach cleanup is definitely not enough to say something is safe," the resident said. Mahajan added, "We can't change what's in the ocean or what people have done in the past, but we can change our reaction to it." Mahajan told CBS News she found syringes, cut straws, syringe plungers, syringe caps and small plastic baggies along the beach. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Fox News Digital reached out to the NJDEP, but the agency declined to comment. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The syringe discovery comes less than two weeks after another unusual scene unfolded along the Jersey Shore, when nearly 30 dead juvenile dogfish sharks were found scattered across a beach in Sea Isle City. At the time, shark ecologist Mike Heithaus told Fox News Digital that seeing so many sharks wash ashore at one time was rare. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The incident did not appear consistent with a widespread toxin or pollution event, Heithaus said, and he suggested the sharks may have been caught and discarded.

articles.title: Dolly Parton, country music icon, dies at 80
articles.summary: The “Queen of Country” won 11 Grammys and sold over 100 million records, making her one of the bestselling performers of all time.
articles.body: Dolly Parton, who rose from a loving if impoverished upbringing in the mountains of East Tennessee to become the “Queen of Country” music, a Hollywood star and a beloved American icon, has died, her family announced Tuesday. She was 80. Her team confirmed the death and said the star had faced a brief battle with cancer and died Tuesday surrounded by her loved ones. Parton’s nephew, Brian Seaver, announced the news in a video posted on her Instagram. “My name is Brian Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next,” Seaver said in a video. “This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it till now,” he added. Seaver added that Parton “lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by [her late husband] Carl, her parents, and countless others.” “Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly — Aunt, Granny, Gigi. May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you,” Seaver said at the end of the video statement. The star’s team honored her legacy, saying she “spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched.” “Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand,” Team Dolly said in a statement Tuesday. “Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact.” As word of Parton’s death spread, the tributes began pouring in. President Donald Trump ordered U.S. flags lowered to half-staff nationwide for one week while a constellation of the entertainment world’s biggest stars weighed in with condolences. Her death comes after Parton announced in May that she was canceling a Las Vegas show and had been undergoing treatment for kidney stones for several years. "Lord, they dig more stones out of me a year than the rock quarry in Rockwood, Tennessee," Parton said in a statement. "But seriously, my immune system and my digestive system got all out of whack over the past couple three years, and they’re working real hard on rebuilding and strengthening those, and hopefully, I’ll be up to snuff again soon." On Friday, Parton acknowledged she had lost a step after her husband, Carl Dean, died in March 2025. But she insisted she wasn’t ready to leave the stage. “Even though I’m still healin’,” Parton told People. “I’m still workin’! You know me — as I’ve often said — I’ve dreamed myself into a corner, and I still have so many things I want to achieve, so I’m gonna keep on working as long as I can to see everything come to life.” During her more than 60-year career, Parton sold over 100 million records and won 11 Grammy Awards, making her one of the bestselling musical performers of all time. Parton also became a star on the silver screen, gaining a whole new audience and critical acclaim when she brought her Southern charm to movies like “9 to 5” (she wrote and sang the theme song), “Steel Magnolias” and "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." Bedecked in blond bouffant hairdos and never without her makeup, Parton also became one of the nation’s best-known brands who parried questions about her hourglass figure and augmented breasts with her signature self-deprecating wit. “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap,” Parton once said. Parton was a shrewd businesswoman who amassed an estimated $650 million fortune and maintained creative control in the cutthroat and male-dominated music industry. She presided over an entertainment empire that included the Dollywood theme park. And she was a devoted philanthropist who launched the Dollywood Foundation to provide poverty relief and fund educational programs in her native East Tennessee. Never shy at expressing her Christian faith, Parton was also a public supporter of the LGBTQ community who advocated for marriage equality and spoke up in defense of transgender people. “I keep saying: If you’re the fine Christian that you think you are, why are you judging people,” Parton said during a 2017 interview with Larry King. “That’s God’s job.” Along those lines, she jokingly told a British outlet a few years earlier: “I think gay couples should be allowed to marry. They should suffer just like us heterosexuals.” Through it all Parton leaned on the love of her life, her husband Carl, who died at 82 and who, from the moment they married in 1966, happily ceded the spotlight to his world-famous wife. “Words can’t do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years,” Parton said in July 2025. Born Jan. 19, 1946, in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River near the town of Sevierville, Parton was the fourth of 12 children. Her father, Robert Lee Parton, could not read or write and often supplemented the family's meager income from their farm by working construction jobs. Her mother, Avie Lee Parton, ran the household and was fond of singing traditional Appalachian ballads. The future superstar said it was her mother who instilled in her a love for music. And it was at church that Parton started performing. By age 13, she was singing on local radio and television shows and made her debut at the Grand Ole Opry, where she met Johnny Cash. “Dolly Parton has one of the most distinctive voices in American pop music,” Katherine Dacey, a professor at the Berklee College of Music, told NBC News before Parton’s death. “Her high soprano voice gets its distinctive character from her fast vibrato and vocal twang.” The day after she graduated from Sevier County High School in 1964, Parton headed to Nashville, where she first made her mark writing songs for other performers, some of them with her uncle Bill Owens. In songs like “Tennessee Homesick Blues” and “Coat of Many Colors,” Parton drew inspiration from her hardscrabble childhood. Three years after leaving school, Parton released her first record, “Hello, I'm Dolly,” and caught the attention of country star Porter Wagoner and became a regular on his shows. Then, in 1974, Parton broke out on her own when she topped the country charts for the first time with a song she wrote and performed called “Jolene.” She later revealed it was inspired by a bank teller who flirted with her husband when they were newlyweds. Her next four singles were also country chart-toppers, and one of them, “I Will Always Love You,” later became a huge hit for Whitney Houston in 1992. Parton also won her first Grammy with a single from that record called “Here You Come Again.” Parton, who earned a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1984, made several more movies and performed around the world, but she always returned to the music that first made her famous — and to the hollers of East Tennessee where she was born and where she and her husband made their home. “Never ignore your roots — your home or your hair,” she once said. In 1986, Parton opened the Dollywood theme park in the Great Smoky Mountains near her hometown. The 165 acres include roller coasters, a bald eagle sanctuary and music and crafts that pay tribute to the region's Appalachian heritage. Parton and her husband never had children. And in public statements, Parton said she “believed that God didn’t mean for me to have kids.” “Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom,” Parton told Oprah Winfrey in 2020. “So I think a big part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work.” Parton also left her fans guessing about her politics, although in 2016 she angered many Republicans by saying that Hillary Clinton was “very qualified” to be president. In an online post, Parton insisted she was not endorsing Clinton or Clinton's then-rival, Donald Trump. “I try not to get political but if I am, I might as well just run myself ‘cause I’ve got the hair for it, it’s huge, and they could always use more boobs in the race,” she wrote. While she generally dodged commenting on partisan politics, Parton was hailed in 2020 for helping to fund research at Vanderbilt University that led to the development of Moderna's Covid vaccine. “My longtime friend Dr. Naji Abumrad, who’s been involved in research at Vanderbilt for many years, informed me that they were making some exciting advancements towards research of the coronavirus for a cure,” Parton tweeted in April 2020, as much of the nation was under lockdown. She added that she would be donating $1 million to the research. Abumrad, who treated Parton when she was in a car accident in 2013, became friends with the country star afterward. “Without a doubt in my mind, her funding made the research toward the vaccine go 10 times faster than it would be without it,” he told The Washington Post in November 2020. Parton's philanthropic legacy also includes the creation of the Imagination Library, which mails free books to children around the world. In the three decades since it was founded, the organization has mailed more than 300 million books to kids around the U.S., as well as Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland. The initiative was inspired by Parton’s father, who was illiterate. Parton often spoke about his intelligence and strength of character but said she believed his inability to read and write held him back. “When I got this idea to do the Imagination Library, I wanted to get Daddy involved in it. I wanted him to help me with that so he could take the pride in that and so he did,” she wrote on her website in 2020. “He got to live long enough to hear the kids call me the Book Lady.”

"Lord, they dig more stones out of me a year than the rock quarry in Rockwood, Tennessee," Parton said in a statement. "But seriously, my immune system and my digestive system got all out of whack over the past couple three years, and they’re working real hard on rebuilding and strengthening those, and hopefully, I’ll be up to snuff again soon." On Friday, Parton acknowledged she had lost a step after her husband, Carl Dean, died in March 2025. But she insisted she wasn’t ready to leave the stage. “Even though I’m still healin’,” Parton told People. “I’m still workin’! You know me — as I’ve often said — I’ve dreamed myself into a corner, and I still have so many things I want to achieve, so I’m gonna keep on working as long as I can to see everything come to life.” During her more than 60-year career, Parton sold over 100 million records and won 11 Grammy Awards, making her one of the bestselling musical performers of all time. Parton also became a star on the silver screen, gaining a whole new audience and critical acclaim when she brought her Southern charm to movies like “9 to 5” (she wrote and sang the theme song), “Steel Magnolias” and "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." Bedecked in blond bouffant hairdos and never without her makeup, Parton also became one of the nation’s best-known brands who parried questions about her hourglass figure and augmented breasts with her signature self-deprecating wit. “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap,” Parton once said. Parton was a shrewd businesswoman who amassed an estimated $650 million fortune and maintained creative control in the cutthroat and male-dominated music industry. She presided over an entertainment empire that included the Dollywood theme park. And she was a devoted philanthropist who launched the Dollywood Foundation to provide poverty relief and fund educational programs in her native East Tennessee. Never shy at expressing her Christian faith, Parton was also a public supporter of the LGBTQ community who advocated for marriage equality and spoke up in defense of transgender people. “I keep saying: If you’re the fine Christian that you think you are, why are you judging people,” Parton said during a 2017 interview with Larry King. “That’s God’s job.” Along those lines, she jokingly told a British outlet a few years earlier: “I think gay couples should be allowed to marry. They should suffer just like us heterosexuals.” Through it all Parton leaned on the love of her life, her husband Carl, who died at 82 and who, from the moment they married in 1966, happily ceded the spotlight to his world-famous wife. “Words can’t do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years,” Parton said in July 2025. Born Jan. 19, 1946, in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River near the town of Sevierville, Parton was the fourth of 12 children. Her father, Robert Lee Parton, could not read or write and often supplemented the family's meager income from their farm by working construction jobs. Her mother, Avie Lee Parton, ran the household and was fond of singing traditional Appalachian ballads. The future superstar said it was her mother who instilled in her a love for music. And it was at church that Parton started performing. By age 13, she was singing on local radio and television shows and made her debut at the Grand Ole Opry, where she met Johnny Cash. “Dolly Parton has one of the most distinctive voices in American pop music,” Katherine Dacey, a professor at the Berklee College of Music, told NBC News before Parton’s death. “Her high soprano voice gets its distinctive character from her fast vibrato and vocal twang.” The day after she graduated from Sevier County High School in 1964, Parton headed to Nashville, where she first made her mark writing songs for other performers, some of them with her uncle Bill Owens. In songs like “Tennessee Homesick Blues” and “Coat of Many Colors,” Parton drew inspiration from her hardscrabble childhood. Three years after leaving school, Parton released her first record, “Hello, I'm Dolly,” and caught the attention of country star Porter Wagoner and became a regular on his shows. Then, in 1974, Parton broke out on her own when she topped the country charts for the first time with a song she wrote and performed called “Jolene.” She later revealed it was inspired by a bank teller who flirted with her husband when they were newlyweds. Her next four singles were also country chart-toppers, and one of them, “I Will Always Love You,” later became a huge hit for Whitney Houston in 1992. Parton also won her first Grammy with a single from that record called “Here You Come Again.” Parton, who earned a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1984, made several more movies and performed around the world, but she always returned to the music that first made her famous — and to the hollers of East Tennessee where she was born and where she and her husband made their home. “Never ignore your roots — your home or your hair,” she once said. In 1986, Parton opened the Dollywood theme park in the Great Smoky Mountains near her hometown. The 165 acres include roller coasters, a bald eagle sanctuary and music and crafts that pay tribute to the region's Appalachian heritage. Parton and her husband never had children. And in public statements, Parton said she “believed that God didn’t mean for me to have kids.” “Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom,” Parton told Oprah Winfrey in 2020. “So I think a big part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work.” Parton also left her fans guessing about her politics, although in 2016 she angered many Republicans by saying that Hillary Clinton was “very qualified” to be president. In an online post, Parton insisted she was not endorsing Clinton or Clinton's then-rival, Donald Trump. “I try not to get political but if I am, I might as well just run myself ‘cause I’ve got the hair for it, it’s huge, and they could always use more boobs in the race,” she wrote. While she generally dodged commenting on partisan politics, Parton was hailed in 2020 for helping to fund research at Vanderbilt University that led to the development of Moderna's Covid vaccine. “My longtime friend Dr. Naji Abumrad, who’s been involved in research at Vanderbilt for many years, informed me that they were making some exciting advancements towards research of the coronavirus for a cure,” Parton tweeted in April 2020, as much of the nation was under lockdown. She added that she would be donating $1 million to the research. Abumrad, who treated Parton when she was in a car accident in 2013, became friends with the country star afterward. “Without a doubt in my mind, her funding made the research toward the vaccine go 10 times faster than it would be without it,” he told The Washington Post in November 2020. Parton's philanthropic legacy also includes the creation of the Imagination Library, which mails free books to children around the world. In the three decades since it was founded, the organization has mailed more than 300 million books to kids around the U.S., as well as Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland. The initiative was inspired by Parton’s father, who was illiterate. Parton often spoke about his intelligence and strength of character but said she believed his inability to read and write held him back. “When I got this idea to do the Imagination Library, I wanted to get Daddy involved in it. I wanted him to help me with that so he could take the pride in that and so he did,” she wrote on her website in 2020. “He got to live long enough to hear the kids call me the Book Lady.”

articles.title: Kurdish-led SDF announces dissolution, integration into Syrian state
articles.summary: The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) Mazloum Abdi announced the dissolution of the group on Tuesday, saying it would be fully inte...
articles.body:
The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) Mazloum Abdi announced the dissolution of the group on Tuesday, saying it would be fully integrated into Syrian state institutions.

In a press statement delivered at the presidential palace in Damascus after a meeting with transitional President Ahmad al-Sharaa, Abdi said the Kurdish Autonomous Administration in north-eastern Syria - established during the country's civil war - would also be dissolved.

Abdi said the SDF's mission had ended and that the group was moving "from the phase of defence to the phase of building Syria."

Abdi said that "all military and civilian formations" affiliated with the SDF and the Kurdish Autonomous Administration would also be integrated into state institutions.

The SDF was formally established in October 2015 and became the main US-backed force fighting Islamic State in north-eastern Syria.

The announcement represents a major step toward ending the separate military and administrative structures that Kurdish-led authorities have maintained in parts of north-eastern Syria since the fall of long-time dictator Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.

Under Assad, Kurds were marginalized and faced restrictions on cultural and linguistic expression, while a 1962 census left tens of thousands without Syrian citizenship.

After government forces withdrew from large parts of north-eastern Syria during the 2011 uprising, Kurdish forces established control over much of the area.

Following the fall of al-Assad in December 2024, Damascus and the Kurdish-led authorities began negotiations over the future of the SDF and the administration of north-eastern Syria.

articles.title: In 1957, Georgia artist Eddie Owens Martin began transforming his inherited farmhouse and seven acres; 29 years of work created six major structures and 900+ feet of painted walls, now preserved as one of Americaâs most significant visionary art environments
articles.summary: US News: In 1957, eccentric folk artist Eddie Owens Martin returned to his rural roots near Buena Vista, Georgia, and began turning a seven-acre family propert.
articles.body: In 1957, eccentric folk artist Eddie Owens Martin returned to his rural roots near Buena Vista, Georgia, and began turning a seven-acre family property into a colourful world of painted totems, geometric designs and tall masonry walls. Over the next 29 years, Martin, who called himself "St. EOM", built six major structures and more than 900 feet of brightly painted walls. The site became what is now considered one of North America's most important visionary art environments. Known as Pasaquan, a name Martin created to mean "the past coming together", the site combines Mesoamerican designs, African patterns, Eastern symbols and futuristic ideas into a highly personal style.From fortune teller to Georgia visionaryBorn in 1908 to a family of rural Georgia sharecroppers, Martin left home for New York City at 14. He spent the next three decades working in the city's nightlife and later became a professional fortune teller. According to biographical records maintained by Columbus State University, Martin experienced powerful spiritual visions while seriously ill in 1935. He said a futuristic being told him to change his life and follow "Pasaquoyanism", a personal spiritual system that linked growing long hair with spiritual energy, harmony with the universe and artistic creation. "You're gon' be the start of somethin' new, and you'll call yourself Saint EOM, and you'll be a Pasaquoyan, the first one in the world," Martin recalled of the vision, according to statements preserved by the Pasaquan Preservation Society. After his mother's death, Martin returned to Marion County in 1957 and began building his vision on the family property. He funded the work through fortune telling and tarot readings for local residents. Without formal architectural plans, he spent decades constructing concrete buildings, circular dance platforms, two-storey pagodas and detailed shrines. "I built this place to have somethin' to identify with, 'cause there's nothin' I see in this society that I identify with or desire to emulate," Martin said in archival interviews preserved by the John Michael Kohler Arts Center.Decay leads to major restorationMartin died in 1986. Local supporters then formed the Pasaquan Preservation Society to protect the unusual site. Despite their efforts, years of extreme weather, high humidity and termite damage badly affected the painted walls and wooden structures. Pasaquan was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2008, recognising its importance as a major example of outsider art. But the site still faced serious physical damage. In late 2013, preservation leaders turned to the Wisconsin-based Kohler Foundation after deciding that a full restoration was beyond the resources available locally. The foundation took responsibility for the site in 2014 and began one of the most complex efforts to restore an American art environment. The two-year project involved specialist conservators from Parma Conservation in Chicago, International Artifacts in California and regional construction teams. Workers repaired damaged masonry foundations, treated extensive termite damage, removed overgrown vegetation and carefully repainted deteriorating surfaces. Historical photographs were used to match the bright colours and designs created by St. EOM.Preserving Pasaquan for the futureAfter the restoration was completed in 2016, the Kohler Foundation donated the seven-acre Pasaquan site to Columbus State University (CSU), securing its future as a public and educational site. Today, Pasaquan is managed through the university's Department of Art. It operates as an educational centre, museum and residency site for visiting artists from around the world. Most of St. EOM's outdoor sculptures and painted walls remain at the original site in Marion County. Some of his paintings, textiles and jewellery are also held in permanent collections at CSU and the John Michael Kohler Arts Center, helping protect his work from potential natural disasters. Pasaquan remains open for self-guided tours, educational programmes and cultural events. The colourful complex stands as a lasting record of Martin's 29-year effort to create his own alternative world from concrete, paint and personal belief.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Surrender within 3 weeks, SC tells ex-Tehelka editor Tarun Tejpal
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday directed former Tehelka editor Tarun Tejpal to first surrender within three weeks, saying that his appeal against con.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday directed former Tehelka editor Tarun Tejpal to first surrender within three weeks, saying that his appeal against conviction and 10-year imprisonment in a rape case would be heard only thereafter.Justice Alok Aradhe rejected Tejpalâs plea for exemption from surrendering and asked him to file a surrender certificate before it. Senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for Tejpal, sought three weeksâ time to surrender, the bench granted him time to surrender.Goa govt opposed his plea for exemption from surrendering and said his appeal was not admissible since he had not filed a separate application seeking exemption from surrender or shown a certificate that he has already surrendered as per Order XXII Rule 5 of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013.The Goa bench of Bombay HC convicted Tejpal under multiple provisions of Indian Penal Code (IPC) and sentenced him to 10 yearsâ rigorous imprisonment each under Sections 376(2)(f) and 376(2)(k), with the sentences to run concurrently.The case relates to two alleged incidents at Grand Hyatt in Goa during Tehelkaâs THiNK Fest in Nov 2013. The high court found the victimâs evidence consistent and credible despite extensive cross-examination. The case against Tejpal involves allegations that he sexually assaulted a junior colleague twice in 2013, in an elevator of a high-end hotel in Goa.The Goa Police subsequently registered an FIR against Tarun Tejpal.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Montana man killed 8 relatives, including 4 kids, at Sunday dinner, a family spokesperson says
articles.summary: A man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, at a Sunday dinner at a home in Billings, Montana, before taking his own life, a spokesperson f...
articles.body:
A man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, at a Sunday dinner at a home in Billings, Montana, before taking his own life, a spokesperson for the family told The Associated Press.

Jennifer Mercer, who set up an online fundraiser to help cover funeral costs and other expenses and was authorized to release details, identified the victims as representing four generations of the blended family, ranging from a great-grandmother in her 90s to a 7-year-old girl.

Police said they responded to the home on Sunday evening and heard gunshots coming from out back, just before the house was completely engulfed in flames. They confirmed multiple fatalities, including one person with a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

David Hiller, a neighbor who lives three doors down from the home, heard what he thought were fireworks just after 6 p.m. on Sunday, and didn't think much of the noise until another neighbor called to warn him about a shooting on the cul-de-sac.

Hiller then rushed outside to find police in tactical gear sheltering behind vehicles, some with long guns, while plumes of black smoke rose from the home.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: What we know about Southwest flight attendant's death in Hawaii
articles.summary: Authorities say no conclusions have been made in the death of Southwest flight attendant Jenny Lupton as Honolulu detectives continue investigating.
articles.body:
The investigation into the death of a Southwest Airlines flight attendant in Waikiki has entered a new phase, with Honolulu police confirming that the department's Homicide Detail is now leading the inquiry.

Jenny Lupton, 50, of Moore, Oklahoma, was found dead on Aug. 20 while on a work layover in Honolulu. The Honolulu Police Department said Aug. 24 that detectives are actively investigating the circumstances surrounding her death but emphasized that they have not confirmed how she died.

Police said investigators are conducting interviews, reviewing and recovering surveillance video and working closely with Lupton's family. Authorities also urged the public to rely on verified information as the investigation continues.

Southwest Airlines confirmed Lupton's death to USA TODAY on Aug. 24, saying she died while in Hawaii during a layover.

Her niece, Hannah Lupton, told USA TODAY that the Honolulu Department of the Medical Examiner informed the family it appeared her aunt fell from the balcony of her 24th-floor room at the Hilton Hawaiian Village in Waikiki. She was found near a contamination bin below the balcony.

Lupton's family has continued to press for answers, saying they do not believe she died by suicide.

USA TODAY contacted the Honolulu Medical Examiner's Office and the Honolulu Police Department for additional information on Aug. 25. Officials have said Lupton's cause and manner of death remain pending.

Why is the Homicide Detail investigating?

The Honolulu Police Department said its Homicide Detail is leading the investigation because the unit handles homicides as well as suspicious, unattended and other unexplained deaths.

Police emphasized that assigning the case to the Homicide Detail does not indicate Lupton's death has been ruled a homicide. Officials said investigators won't publicly discuss additional details because the inquiry is ongoing.

Lupton's family has voiced concerns about the flight attendant's unexpected death.

"We are worried that there is possible foul play involved," Hannah Lupton previously told USA TODAY. Officials have not publicly said they suspect a specific cause.

Her sister, Tresa Lupton, told Oklahoma-based television station KFOR that the family believes she either died after "some kind of freak accident or someone harmed her."

Hannah Lupton also described her aunt as "the life of the party," saying she loved her family, her 15-year-old son and her hometown of Moore, Oklahoma.

A GoFundMe campaign set up by Lupton's coworkers to assist her family had raised over $10,900 toward a $26,000 goal as of Aug. 25.

Police have not announced a timeline for completing the investigation, saying it "will take time" as detectives continue gathering evidence.

Lupton's family plans to travel to Hawaii to bring her body home to Oklahoma and work with officials.

The office of the Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond said it has been in contact with the Hawaii Attorney General to help ensure a thorough investigation and remains in communication with Lupton's family, who "deserve to have answers about this tragedy."

Southwest Airlines said in a statement that it is "engaged with local authorities as they investigate" and has offered its condolences to Lupton's family and coworkers.

Reporter Anthony Thompson can be reached at ajthompson@usatodayco.com or on X @athompsonUSAT

articles.title: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
articles.summary: Fuel companies are urging customers not to linger at the pumps after a wave of deadly attacks.
articles.body:
"Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.

Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.

Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.

At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").

In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.

Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound.

"You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.

According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.

One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (£14,500) and $50,000 (£36,000).

"One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."

Some key roads have no functioning petrol stations left, such as the road linking the two major cities of Kharkiv and Dnipro.

All the petrol stations have been destroyed around Opishnya, a large village in neighbouring Poltava region.

"You can see our enemy's strategy. They want to deprive us of fuel," says village chief Mykola Riznyk. In a video on Facebook, he says local authorities have begun stocking up on fuel, keeping small amounts of it in different locations.

In Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine, local resident and driver Kateryna Stokolya says petrol stations everywhere are becoming far stricter about not working during air alerts.

"Now everyone's making allowances for that, and it's not a problem," she tells the BBC. "Security comes first. If you can't fill up now, you'll fill up later. There are no queues or panic buying."

Stokolya believes that, in carrying out attacks of this nature, Russia's intended goal is "terrorising the public so we force the government to capitulate or accept agreements that do not favour Ukraine".

In Ukrainian-controlled areas of the partly occupied Kherson region, almost half the petrol stations have stopped working. The others get attacked by Russian drones "almost every day", says deputy regional administration head Oleksandr Tolokonnikov.

All petrol stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trostyanets, a town of almost 20,000 people near the north-eastern border with Russia. In response, local authorities started dispensing fuel straight from road tankers which keep changing their location to minimise the chances of being hit.

Ukrainians appear to be heeding the advice of authorities.

"Clients aren't browsing the aisles anymore, looking at what we've got on our shelves," says Oleksandr Melnychuk, head of the strategic marketing department at BRSM Nafta chain of petrol stations. "They fill up and are keen to get on their way as soon as possible."

His company has lost eight petrol stations and is rebuilding another two after they were hit.

To protect customers, BRSM Nafta has been building concrete shelters at its forecourts and also covering them in anti-drone nets. It has also shortened working hours and reduced the number of staff present in some locations.

However, so far the drone strikes have not had a dramatic impact on fuel supplies. According to a report by the National Bank of Ukraine, 4% of the country's filling stations have been damaged or destroyed, but the impact on the market has been small.

"Increasing sales in regions which are further away from the front line or from the border with Russia have made up for sales lost at destroyed stations," the report says.

The picture in Russia is very different, after Ukraine's campaign of attacks on Russian refineries and other infrastructure.

Russia has seen fuel shortages in almost every region as a result. One popular newspaper in Russia, Izvestia, said last week that petrol was only available at 28% of Russian filling stations.

Unlike in Russia, Ukraine does not rely on vulnerable large refineries and fuel depots, instead importing fuel by road using tanker trucks.

Ukraine's market is also saturated with numerous petrol stations, which usually offer drivers alternatives should one or several of them be targeted in a particular area, Sirenko says.

"You curse and drive on to another petrol station. OK, you travel for 10km more than you bargained for, but that's not such a big problem," he says.

If anything, it is the war between the US and Iran that is having a bigger impact on local fuel prices, he says. Normally, the most expensive parts of filling stations are left undamaged by Russian attacks, such as petrol and diesel tanks underground.

articles.title: Miami Dolphins Discussion: Who Must Shine Edition
articles.summary: We ask Dolphins fans which players must show out in Friday’s preseason game against the Falcons to make the roster.
articles.body:
As our Miami Dolphins continue to progress through the final days of training camp, following two joint sessions, and two preseason games, the front office has all but finalized the 53-man roster for the 2026-2027 NFL season, with their biggest questions to answer being those players that sit at the bottom of the roster. Like every year, the team features a mix of new free-agent signings and draft picks during offseason work and training camp. This period always brings its share of surprises: some highly anticipated players struggle to find their footing, while unexpected standouts emerge to exceed all expectations.

So this evening's Phinsider Question Of The Day is:

Which Miami Dolphins player or players who you and/or others believed were shoe in's for the Dolphins 2026-2027 roster who now must show something above and beyond what we have seen from them thus far in camp and the preseason if they have any hope of making the final 53-man roster and why?

Please share your thoughts and answers in the comments section below-
